content:
Several 3D-printable storage systems can work together, but they solve different problems. Gridfinity is mainly for small items in drawers; Neogrid creates larger compartments; openGrid provides mounting boards; Underware routes cables.
Four systems at a glance openGrid Gridfinity Neogrid Underware Image: Hands On Katie Image: MakerWorld — Gavin F Image: Hands On Katie Image: MakerWorld — Underware 2.0 System Best suited to Basic approach openGrid Walls, workbench sides and other mounting surfaces Printable 28 mm grid panels and snap-in holders. Developed by David D, with an expanding accessory ecosystem. Gridfinity Drawers, shelves and desktops 42 × 42 mm baseplates with rearrangeable bins and tool holders. Created by Zack Freedman. Neogrid Larger items and configurable drawer compartments 3D-printed X/T/L/I junctions hold strips of MDF, uPVC or acrylic. Connectors are available for openGrid or Gridfinity bases. Underware Cables and optional LED strips Printable snap-together cable channels. Can mount on openGrid or directly to suitable surfaces. Katie’s organisation overview is a useful starting point for understanding the systems together; the openGrid project documentation explains the underlying board and snap mechanism.
How to combine them A mixed drawer: use Gridfinity bins for screws and small components, with Neogrid dividers for bulkier objects. Neogrid has versions designed for a Gridfinity baseplate, so the complete drawer does not need to be converted to openGrid.
A drawer based on openGrid: choose openGrid boards as the common base and attach Neogrid connectors. This is a supported Neogrid variant, not a speculative adaptation. Where small Gridfinity bins are needed, use an openGrid-to-Gridfinity adapter. See Neogrid on openGrid for the actual parts and assembly approach.
A workbench or tool wall: use openGrid for lightweight, frequently rearranged accessories. Gridfinity bins can sit on compatible shelves or adapters. Route cables underneath the bench with Underware channels, mounted to openGrid or directly to the surface.
Heavy tool storage: a French-cleat wall made from wood is a complementary option for heavier items; it is not a plug-in accessory standard for openGrid.
For a concrete example of how the systems fit, see Neogrid on openGrid.
What is actually compatible? openGrid and Gridfinity have different grids: 28 mm versus 42 mm. Their pitches coincide every 84 mm, but the attachment profiles are different. To use Gridfinity bins on an openGrid base, look for a dedicated compatible shelf or adapter. Neogrid has multiple connector variants. Select the version for the base being used (openGrid or Gridfinity). The default divider connectors are intended for approximately 8.5 mm sheet material; measure the actual divider material before printing. Underware is a cable-management subsystem, not a bin system. It can be integrated into the same workspace, particularly through openGrid mountings, without implying that its parts attach directly to Gridfinity bins. For the actual mounting method and adapter geometry, follow the specific model’s documentation rather than assuming that two products with a similar grid are interchangeable.
Other systems worth knowing Multiboard — another modular 3D-printed wall-board system, with its own mounts and accessories. Check adapters rather than assuming direct compatibility with openGrid. Honeycomb Storage Wall (HSW) — hexagonal 3D-printed wall panels and holders, a distinct mounting ecosystem. French cleats — simple wooden rails for heavier wall-mounted workshop storage. Related saved ideas: Plywood Sorting Cases, Eurobox Dividers and Cargo Organisers.
These are reference systems, not a chosen or tested workshop installation.

content:
Could a compact microcontroller board with a round display and a six-axis motion sensor provide visual feedback to help keep a handheld drill at the intended angle? This is an idea to explore, not a planned build.
Inspiration: Copilot Drilling Image: Copilot Drilling Copilot Drilling is a commercial drill-mounted alignment aid. A ring of coloured LEDs indicates how to correct the drill’s angle. The retrofit version fits to the rear of a drill using an adapter, and a zero function supports a chosen reference orientation.
The interesting part is the simple, immediately visible feedback during drilling, rather than showing an angle as a number.
For a visual explanation of aligning a drill with the surface of the workpiece, see this YouTube Short.
Another approach: laser circles Image: BullseyeBore BullseyeBore Core takes a different approach to drill alignment: instead of a sensor and display, it projects laser circles onto the surface being drilled.
As the drill chuck rotates, one laser beam parallel to the drill bit traces a reference circle on the workpiece. A second beam, aimed at an angle, traces an alignment circle.
Drill square to the surface: the rings share the same centre (concentric). Drill tilted: the alignment ring becomes offset and more elliptical relative to the reference ring. Why two circles? The point is not to measure their diameter. It is easier to see whether the rings share one centre than to judge whether a single projected circle is slightly distorted.
Simple schematic of the alignment principle, not a drawing of the product.
This is a useful contrast to the ESP32 idea: the lasers compare the drill directly with the actual workpiece surface, even if that surface is sloping. They do not need an IMU or a separate sensor against the wall, but the drill must be turning for the rings to appear.
Concept A small, removable electronic drill alignment guide fitted to the back of a cordless drill. A motion sensor measures the drill’s orientation, while a round screen shows an intuitive digital bubble or moving crosshair to help the user maintain a chosen drilling angle. A zero/calibration action could set a gravity-based reference angle; a 3D-printed mount would connect the device to the drill.
This is an initial design concept, not a tested solution. In particular, it remains to be explored how the reference angle, sensor-to-bit calibration and on-screen feedback would work in practice.
Display idea Original UI concept illustration, not a screenshot or tested design.
A moving dot approaches the centre of a crosshair; the indicator changes from red to yellow to green as the drill approaches the chosen orientation. This is just one possible interface for the round display.
Possible hardware The smaller Waveshare RP2350-Touch-LCD-1.46 is an interesting alternative to the larger ESP32-S3 board. Both use the same QMI8658 six-axis sensor (accelerometer and gyroscope), so the basic angle-measuring capability is comparable.
Image: Waveshare Image: Waveshare RP2350-Touch-LCD-1.46 ESP32-S3-Touch-LCD-2.1 Screen 1.46-inch round touch LCD, 412 × 412 2.1-inch round touch LCD, 480 × 480 Motion sensor QMI8658 6DOF QMI8658 6DOF Approximate outside diameter 45 mm 75 mm Wireless connectivity No built-in Wi-Fi/Bluetooth Wi-Fi and Bluetooth LE Battery connection 3.7 V Li-ion connection and charge management Li-ion connection and charge management Manufacturer-listed board price US$20.99–22.99 US$32.99 Prices are manufacturer’s listed board prices observed on 5 November 2026; shipping and taxes are not included.
For a standalone graphical drill-angle indicator, the RP2350 should have ample capability: read the IMU and draw the crosshair, angle and zero-setting controls. It is smaller and less expensive. The ESP32-S3 becomes more interesting if a wireless second sensor is ever considered; RP2350 would require additional connectivity hardware for that approach.
References: RP2350 product and examples · ESP32-S3 product and documentation. A 3D-printed drill attachment and battery would still need to be designed for either board.
Practical drilling situations The question is not whether the Waveshare has the same buttons as Copilot, but whether it can help maintain the intended drilling direction. With a six-axis accelerometer/gyroscope and a round display, the same basic principle appears feasible: set a reference and show the deviation while drilling.
Original schematic: each drilling direction is shown from two perpendicular viewpoints.
Drilling situation How to set the reference DIY guide with one motion sensor Straight down into a flat board (90°) Use the vertical direction. Yes. Gravity provides a stable reference. 45° into a flat board Hold the drill at the desired 45° angle and facing the desired direction, then press zero. Yes in principle. The screen can show how the drill deviates from that starting position. Straight into a vertical wall (90°) First set a direction perpendicular to the wall, then press zero. Yes in principle. Merely holding the drill horizontally is not enough; the wall-facing direction must be set first. Angled hole into a wall or sloping board Set the intended direction against a reference, then zero. Yes in principle, once that complete starting orientation has been established. What does Copilot do differently? Copilot 2 already has a finished, calibrated sensor system, clear LED guidance, a rechargeable battery and a mounting system. Its five-second delayed zero lets the user put the back of the device against a workpiece to set a perpendicular reference. It does not automatically know the orientation of the surface.
A DIY version could follow this idea with a zero button and a moving dot on the screen. The accelerometer provides a stable gravity reference; the gyroscope tracks rotations away from the chosen orientation. Changes in direction that gravity cannot determine will slowly drift when calculated from the gyroscope, so the performance over a drilling operation needs testing. Copilot’s specific internal sensor is not published, and there is no evidence here that an additional sensor type is necessary to reproduce the basic functionality.
Related DIY references No documented DIY drill alignment guide using a screen for live feedback has been found yet. The examples below cover parts of the idea, but not the same combination of drill mounting, IMU-based orientation and graphical feedback.
Build a Drill Position Indicator — Circuit Cellar (2021): the closest example found. A battery-powered drill alignment indicator built around an Arduino Nano, MPU-6050 IMU and LEDs, mounted in the drill’s support handle. Planum — a Digital Spirit Level Tool (2025): a working digital level made with a Waveshare ESP32-S3 1.28-inch round display, six-axis IMU, battery and a 3D-printed enclosure. Not a drill guide, but a particularly relevant display/sensor example. Humanix LA100 — GitHub: an open-source digital inclinometer using an Arduino Nano, MPU6050, OLED and laser. Another reference for sensor readout and calibration, not a drill attachment. The drill-specific example uses LEDs; the display-based examples are general inclinometers or digital levels, not drill-mounted alternatives.
Status: idea and reference links saved; no hardware selected, code written or prototype tested.
summary: A drill alignment guide using a round display and a built-in six-axis motion sensor, with Waveshare RP2350 and ESP32-S3 hardware options.

Source: TMAT Europe Trunk organizer mat Published 19 May 2026. 3D-printable, piece-by-piece modular mat by Tora. Because the parts are generated from source, layouts and dimensions can be changed rather than relying only on the supplied printable files. It is not an OpenSCAD project.

Diagnosis: possible next steps Without opening the appliance One power reset, if not already done. If there is no smell, visible damage or tripping breaker, disconnect via the accessible plug or circuit breaker for about 10 seconds, then restore power once. This is the reset in the Siemens instruction manual. Do not repeatedly reset a breaker that trips. Check the remaining signs of life. Does the interior light come on when the door opens? Any fan, beep or display activity? Note these observations without repeatedly trying to heat. Record the circumstances. Which function was operating (microwave, hot air, grill or steam)? Any pop, smell, or breaker trip at the moment it went black? Since the breaker and socket were checked, do not start the investigation by repeating those two checks. If the external supply is confirmed and the appliance remains completely dark after one safe reset, professional diagnosis is the next step.
For a qualified technician A reasonable fault-isolation approach is to check the power entering the appliance, protective devices, the mains input path, internal low-voltage power supply and control/display electronics. If a protective fuse or thermal cut-out has operated, the underlying cause also needs to be established. Verify the actual failed part and its compatibility with revision /03 before ordering it.
These are areas to investigate, not a diagnosis. A faulty inverter, control board, thermal protection or mains filter has not been established from the symptom alone.
Safety: this appliance contains a microwave high-voltage circuit. Siemens explicitly warns not to remove its housing. High-voltage components can remain dangerous even after unplugging. Internal inspection, measurements, bypassing protection and board replacement must be left to a qualified specialist.
How can it be repaired, and what does it cost? Siemens service Siemens Netherlands repair service and the Siemens tariff graphic give an out-of-warranty starting price of €149 for a visit/assessment and a repair without replacement parts. The initial diagnosis is included in the starting charge; it is not a second €149 fee.
If parts are required, the tariff is €149 + part costs + additional labour, with €14.90 per six minutes shown in the graphic. Siemens provides a quotation before proceeding.
One detail to confirm when booking: if a repair estimate is declined, is the fee exactly the €149 starting charge? The published pricing graphic does not spell out that case separately.
The published age discount applies only under certain conditions. FD 9902 means production in February 2019, about 7 years and 9 months before this memo. The purchase date is unknown; any discount must be confirmed with Siemens rather than assumed.
Independent repair service A qualified microwave/appliance repairer is another option. Ask upfront about diagnosis charges, original BSH spare parts, labour, the quotation process, and the charge if the repair is declined. Do not buy a speculative controller board in advance.
Questions still open Has a deliberate power reset been tried since the failure? Does the interior light come on with the door open? Which function was running when the display suddenly went black? Was there a noise, smell, or breaker trip at the moment of failure? Can we obtain the exact /03 power-control PCB part number or a professional service diagram? The HUB75 enclosure may need printed frame connectors, corner protectors, hinges and other fittings. The display is used outdoors once per year. The material choice is mainly about where a part sits on the same display: internal fittings support the structure, while external parts are more likely to be bumped during handling and transport.
Current direction, not a final decision: use PETG for printed parts inside the display and PCTG for parts on the outside, especially corner protectors. PCTG is considered for its impact toughness, not because it is automatically more weather-resistant. ASA is included for comparison, but is not currently needed for the intended use.
Material comparison Material Character Main trade-off HUB75 application PLA Relatively stiff and simple to print Can crack under impact; poor heat tolerance Reference material and fit prototypes, not preferred for outdoor fittings PETG Tough, slightly yielding, easy to print Lower rigidity than PLA; heat and long-term UV exposure need attention First choice for internal frame joints and brackets PETG-CF Carbon-fibre-filled PETG: stiffer and dimensionally stable Abrasive filament; stiffness does not guarantee impact toughness or layer strength Only where extra rigidity is needed PCTG Tough copolyester, often with excellent resistance to impact Higher printing temperatures; price and UV performance vary by brand Preferred candidate for external corners and fittings that may be knocked ASA Good heat, sunlight and weather resistance Printing is more demanding; ventilation and an enclosure recommended Reference material; not preferred for this display’s occasional outdoor use TPU (e.g. 95A) Elastomeric, flexible and shock absorbing Too compliant for most structural joints Separate bumpers, feet, pads or seals Stiffness, strength, impact resistance and flexibility These properties describe different things:
Stiffness: resistance to bending. A higher flexural modulus (MPa) means less deflection for the same shape and load. Strength: the maximum load or stress the material can carry before it fails. Impact resistance (slagvastheid): the ability to take a sudden hit without breaking. Izod and Charpy tests measure the energy absorbed when a test specimen is struck, often reported in kJ/m². Elongation at break: how far a specimen stretches before fracture. High elongation or impact resistance does not make a material rubber-like. For example, a PLA corner may hold its shape but fracture during a sharp knock. A tougher PCTG corner may deform more before breaking. A TPU bumper is a different solution: it can deliberately compress and absorb impact energy. Impact-resistant and shock-absorbing are not interchangeable.
The printed part also depends on geometry, wall thickness, screw holes and layer orientation. Tests on different specimen shapes, standards or print directions are not directly comparable.
Stiffness comparison The following are Bambu Lab’s own XY-direction bending-modulus results for printed specimens, not universal values for a material family.
Bambu Lab filament Flexural modulus Relative to PLA PETG-CF 2,910 MPa 106% PLA 2,750 MPa 100% PETG HF 2,050 MPa 75% ASA 1,920 MPa 70% Source: Bambu Lab Filament Guide (PDF). The PETG figure is specifically for PETG HF, not a universal PETG value. A manufacturer’s values may change with the formulation and test method.
In this dataset, PETG-CF is only about 6% stiffer than PLA, while ASA is approximately 30% less stiff than PLA. A more flexible response to bending does not automatically mean better impact resistance.
For context, Fiberlogy PCTG specifies a 1,600 MPa flexural modulus (ISO 178). It is deliberately not placed in the Bambu Lab ranking: the supplier’s test data and the Bambu printed-specimen data are not a like-for-like comparison.
Why try PCTG? The Fiberlogy PCTG technical datasheet lists:
Property Fiberlogy PCTG Test Notched Izod impact strength at 23 °C 92 kJ/m² ISO 180 Flexural modulus 1,600 MPa ISO 178 Elongation at break 220% ISO 527 Heat-deflection temperature at 0.45 MPa 76 °C ISO 75 Heat-deflection temperature at 1.8 MPa 64 °C ISO 75 Fiberlogy also quotes a PETG reference range of 5–8 kJ/m² in a notched Izod test on its product page. This supports testing PCTG for parts that might be knocked or dropped. It does not mean that a printed PCTG corner will necessarily be twenty times stronger than a PETG corner. The actual geometry and print-layer bonds must be tested.
These figures are specific to Fiberlogy. A PCTG spool from another brand should not be assumed to have identical stiffness, elongation or impact resistance. PCTG is not automatically more heat-resistant or UV-resistant than other materials either.
Printing example: Fiberlogy recommends 250–270 °C nozzle, approximately 90 °C bed and drying at 60 °C for 4 hours. Follow the profile for the selected brand and check the printer’s temperature capability.
Internal versus external parts The initial plan is one HUB75 display with two possible filament choices according to the part’s location:
Location on display Candidate Why Inside the enclosure PETG Practical to print; suitable starting point for panel mounts, brackets and frame connectors that are protected by the enclosure Outside the enclosure PCTG Attractive for corner protectors, external fittings and other pieces that may take knocks during assembly, transport or use This is a working material selection, not yet a tested design. It does not mean all external parts must use PCTG, or that PCTG is automatically more flexible than PETG in every formulation.
Occasional outdoor use The display will be used outside once per year, rather than permanently installed outdoors. Long-term UV ageing is therefore not the main reason to choose a filament. On this basis, there is no particular reason to switch to ASA now.
For that outdoor event, the practical questions are whether the printed parts tolerate rain, knocks during handling, and possible heat from direct sun. Pay particular attention to the internal temperature of a dark enclosure if the PETG parts carry sustained loads.
Keeping water out of the electronics is an enclosure design issue: seals, cable entries, condensation and cooling need attention regardless of whether the printed parts use PETG or PCTG.
PCTG manufacturers and buying options PCTG is available from several brands, even though it was not identified as a Bambu Lab- or eSUN-branded product in the manufacturer catalogues checked in November 2026. Bambu Lab sells PETG variants, PETG-CF and ASA; eSUN lists PETG and PETG+HS alternatives, but these are not PCTG. Third-party PCTG can be used where the printer supports the required temperatures and settings.
Brand / filament Reference Indicative listing Why consider it Fiberlogy PCTG Manufacturer / technical data · 3DJake selection €32.49 / 1 kg Detailed impact, stiffness and elongation figures; a useful test reference 3DJake PCTG PCTG Black €30.49 / 1 kg Straightforward EU-supplied alternative, with downloadable datasheet Spectrum Premium PCTG Manufacturer · 3DJake selection €26.49 / 1 kg (selected colours) Another candidate with published technical information FormFutura AthenaX Manufacturer · AthenaX detail From €28.92 (size varies) Engineering PCTG; multiple spool sizes ROSA3D PCTG Manufacturer / products €21.93 / 1 kg refill (selected colours) Lower-priced refill option, with its own datasheet Prices are indicative product listings, not verified checkout totals or guaranteed availability. Spool weight and refill packaging vary, and prices may change. The links are retained for checking again before purchase.
Extrudr PCTG is another possible brand to compare. The fact that several brands are sold as PCTG does not establish equivalent mechanical performance.
For third-party filament on a Bambu printer, also check spool/AMS fit and a suitable material profile. Fiberlogy provides a Bambu Lab profile on its PCTG product page.
Provisional choice by component Component Starting material Reason / alternative Structural frame connector PETG Use PCTG if impact failure appears; PETG-CF only for a demonstrated stiffness need Rigid mounting bracket PETG Evaluate screw clamping and warm-weather creep External corner protector PCTG Preferred candidate for impact resistance during handling and transport Internal clip or gently flexing part PETG PCTG if impact toughness or repeated flexing warrants testing; check layer direction Soft corner bumper or gasket TPU or dedicated seal Better for deliberate cushioning, not a structural connector Working recommendation: PETG inside, PCTG outside. Start with PETG for internal brackets and frame connections; print an external corner protector in PCTG (Fiberlogy as a well-documented candidate, with 3DJake or Spectrum as alternatives). Test fit, screw stress, impact and handling. The selection remains provisional until the actual parts are tested.

This page collects 3D-printable hinge ideas and real-world mechanism references for the HUB75 display enclosure.
The examples are starting points rather than final selections. The main questions are how far the panel must open, whether the hinge should remain hidden when closed, and how much clearance the mechanism needs around the enclosure edge.
Stop and 180-degree hinges Stop hinge MakerWorld — Stop Hinge A printable hinge with an integrated stop that limits its maximum opening angle. Source: MakerWorld This may be useful for a lid or support panel that must stop at a defined angle without a separate cable or support arm.
180-degree strong hinge MakerWorld — 180° Strong Hinge, 36 mm A relatively large external hinge with an opening range of up to 180 degrees; the linked version is identified as a 36 mm model. Source: MakerWorld This is a simple reference when maximum opening angle matters more than hiding the mechanism.
180-degree opening gate hinge MakerWorld — 180° Opening Gate Hinge, PETG A gate-style PETG hinge designed to open up to 180 degrees, with accessible external mounting points. Source: MakerWorld The exposed mounting points make this mechanically straightforward, but it would remain visible on the outside of the enclosure.
Multi-link and concealed hinges Multi-link hinges use several pivoting links to control both rotation and translation of a lid or panel.
That extra movement can move the panel away from the enclosure while it opens, which may help clear an overlapping edge, raised rim or seal.
Hidden hinge MakerWorld — Hidden Hinge A concealed multi-link hinge intended to remain hidden when the connected parts are closed. Source: MakerWorld The mechanism moves the panel while it rotates and therefore needs recesses and sufficient internal clearance.
180-degree concealed hinge Thingiverse — 180 Degree Concealed Hinge A concealed linkage design with an opening range of up to 180 degrees. Source: Thingiverse This is an interesting reference if the panel should open almost flat while the hinge stays hidden when closed.
Print-in-place concealed hinge MakerWorld — Print-in-Place Concealed Hinge A concealed multi-link mechanism printed as a complete moving assembly. Source: MakerWorld Although presented as a fidget model, it is useful as a reference for print-in-place clearances and linkage movement.
PIP hinge for interior doors MakerWorld — PIP Hinge for Interior Doors A larger remix of the print-in-place concealed hinge, adapted for lightweight doors or panels. Source: MakerWorld This shows how the same linkage principle can be developed from a small mechanism into a larger functional hinge.
3D-printable spider hinge Cults3D — Spider Hinge A printable interpretation of a spider-hinge mechanism that moves the panel away from the enclosure while it opens. Source: Cults3D The motion could help clear an overlapping edge or seal. For a larger or more heavily loaded version, metal pins or bolts may be more suitable than printed pivots.
Real-world spider hinge references The following commercial metal hinges are included only to understand real spider-hinge geometry, movement and construction. They are not currently proposed as parts for the display enclosure.
Osculati spider hinge Osculati — Spider Hinge A commercial metal spider hinge showing how linked arms move a panel away from the enclosure while it opens. Source: Osculati This is especially useful as a reference for pivot placement and the compact folded geometry of a real metal mechanism.
Timage slim spider hinge Timage — Slim Spider Hinge with Pin Lock A slim handed spider hinge with an opening angle of approximately 178 degrees and a pin lock for the open position. Source: Timage The pin lock is an interesting additional idea if the enclosure lid ever needs to stay mechanically secured in its fully open position.
What to compare next For the enclosure design, the most useful next comparison is likely:
simple external hinge — easiest to build and strongest, but visible; concealed multi-link hinge — cleaner outside appearance, but needs more internal room; spider hinge — useful when the panel must move away from an overlapping edge before rotating; integrated stop or lock — useful if the lid needs a defined working/open position.

When developing a Hugo site in Visual Studio Code, the local Hugo server can automatically rebuild pages as files change. Sometimes the browser still shows an older version of a stylesheet because it has cached the CSS file.
Reload the browser without using cached CSS In the browser showing the local Hugo preview (for example, Chrome or Edge on Windows), press:
Ctrl + Shift + R
This performs a hard reload, requesting fresh page resources instead of reusing the usual browser cache. It is a browser shortcut, not a VS Code shortcut.
This can help when a CSS change appears briefly but disappears again, or when the page does not reflect the latest styling even though the Hugo files are up to date.
If that does not help, open the browser’s Developer Tools, go to Network, enable Disable cache, and reload the page. This option normally applies only while Developer Tools stays open.
Note: A hard reload only addresses browser caching. If the change is still missing, also check whether Hugo is serving the expected working directory and branch.

Problem NetBeans runs with Java 21, but Maven builds use Java 8.
NetBeans can use separate Java versions for the IDE itself and for Maven. Changing the IDE’s netbeans_jdkhome setting does not automatically change Maven’s JDK.
Solution Open Tools → Options → Java → Maven → Default JDK and select the JDK you want Maven to use.
In this case, Default JDK was still set to JDK 1.8, even though the IDE was running on Java 21. Selecting JDK 21 addresses that configuration mismatch.
To check, run a Maven build and look at the JAVA_HOME value shown in the NetBeans output. The IDE sets this value for its Maven command, so it does not necessarily come from the Windows PATH.
If the intended JDK is not listed, register it under Tools → Java Platforms.

Yes — Neogrid can be mounted directly on openGrid. Neogrid has connector variants designed to clip into the openGrid base. This is a supported arrangement described by Hands On Katie, not something that needs a separately designed adapter.
How it works Image: Hands On Katie — Neogrid An openGrid baseplate covers the drawer bottom. Small printed Neogrid X, T, L and I connectors attach to that base and hold upright dividers cut from sheet material. This makes larger compartments without 3D-printing the entire walls.
Katie recommends openGrid for its firmer attachment of the dividers. She also provides variants for a Gridfinity base, which hold a little less firmly but work with existing Gridfinity drawers.
Parts and fitting Base: print openGrid tiles to suit the drawer. openGrid’s basic grid pitch is 28 mm. Connectors: select the openGrid-compatible Neogrid connector type, not the Gridfinity-specific variant. Use X junctions for intersections, T junctions for branches, L corners and I pieces for straight joins. Divider material: thin MDF, uPVC utility board or acrylic. The standard Neogrid connectors target approximately 8.5 mm material thickness; measure your sheet and print a test connector first. Spacing: follow the Neogrid guide for divider cut lengths on an openGrid base. Do not reuse dimensions calculated for a 42 mm Gridfinity layout. A configurable alternative is NeoGrid 2.0 by BlackjackDuck, which can generate connectors for an openGrid base, a Gridfinity base, or no grid. It is useful when the divider thickness or compartment layout differs from the original files.
Combining with Gridfinity Gridfinity bins need a compatible openGrid-to-Gridfinity adapter or holder; they do not clip into openGrid in the same way as Neogrid connectors. The pitches differ: 28 mm for openGrid and 42 mm for Gridfinity. Their dimensions align every 84 mm (3 openGrid cells = 2 Gridfinity cells), which can help plan adapter regions.
For example, a drawer could use Neogrid dividers for hand tools and a small adapted Gridfinity area for screws without replacing the openGrid base.
References: Hands On Katie — Neogrid · Hands On Katie — openGrid · NeoGrid 2.0 on MakerWorld.
This is a saved design approach; the combination has not been built or tested for this site.

A prototype concept for distributing 5 V power from one supply to the HUB75 LED matrix panels.
Proposed concept The prototype is deliberately simple:
1 × removable 20 A input for the main 5 V supply; 2 × 4-pole barrier-strip terminals for the HUB75 panel outputs; 1 × additional 2-pole 10 A screw terminal for PCB / auxiliary 5 V; all mounted on a 4 × 6 cm double-sided experiment PCB. The two 4-pole barrier strips provide eight screw positions in total. Five positions are intended for the five HUB75 panel feeds, leaving three spare positions.
The removable 20 A connector is only the main input. The PCB-side connector is the 90° male part, so the supply cable plugs in from the edge of the board. The matching female screw-terminal plug stays attached to the power-supply cable.
Prototype parts The illustrations below are project-owned schematic drawings stored locally with the Hugo page, not copied vendor product photos. Each illustration links to the relevant product page.
Part Product 1 × prototype PCB — TinyTronics 4 × 6 cm double-sided board, 2.54 mm grid and 1 mm holes. 2 × 4-pole barrier terminals — one complete 4-pole strip per row. 7.62 mm pitch, M3 screws, 33 × 14 × 15 mm, rated up to 20 A. 20 A input — PCB side — Kangnex WJ2EDGR-5.08-2P, 90°, 2-pole, 5.08 mm. 20 A input — cable side — Kangnex WJ2EDGK-5.08-2P removable female plug. The 5 V supply cable stays screwed into this connector. 1 × auxiliary terminal — standard 2-pole 5.08 mm screw terminal, rated up to 10 A, for PCB / auxiliary 5 V. Reference examples The commercial boards that inspired this layout are kept on a separate page so they do not get mixed up with the actual prototype design:
Power distribution examples
The examples page contains the original product links and small, clickable reference thumbnails where an exact product image could be verified.
Electrical construction The experiment PCB is mainly a convenient mechanical carrier. The small copper pads and plated holes should not be used as the main high-current distribution path.
A practical prototype would use two substantial conductors on the underside:
one continuous +5 V bus; one continuous GND bus. Each pole of the two barrier strips then gets a short connection to the appropriate power bus. Thick tinned copper wire or another suitably dimensioned bus conductor is preferable to trying to carry the combined panel current through the small prototyping-board pads.
The input connector, bus conductors and supply wiring must all be dimensioned for the combined current of the complete display, not just the current of one panel.
Mechanical checks before building There is one important point to verify before ordering the complete set.
The 4 × 6 cm experiment PCB has 1 mm round holes. The TinyTronics 4-pole 7.62 mm barrier terminal uses 1.1 mm rectangular pins and TinyTronics explicitly marks that connector as not experiment-PCB friendly. The 20 A PCB-side input connector uses 1.0 mm square pins.
So the 2.54 mm / 7.62 mm pitch alignment is convenient, but the physical pin fit still needs to be checked. Possible solutions are:
carefully enlarging the required prototype-board holes; selecting a prototype board with slightly larger holes; or moving directly to a small custom PCB after confirming the layout. The first prototype should also confirm that the complete 2 × 4-pole barrier-strip arrangement plus input and auxiliary connector physically fits on 60 × 40 mm with enough room for cable lugs and screwdriver access.

Practical commands for everyday Git work. Steps that depend on GitHub are explicitly labelled.
Clone a repository Open the terminal in Visual Studio Code and choose the parent directory before cloning:
cd C:\projects git clone <repository-url> GitHub example: include the account name in the HTTPS URL when you work with multiple GitHub accounts:
git clone https://username@github.com/username/repository-name.git Open the checkout in Visual Studio Code and inspect the configured remote:
cd repository-name code . git remote -v The username in the URL identifies the intended account; authentication is handled separately, normally by Git Credential Manager.
Change the origin remote URL When a repository is renamed or moved, update its local origin remote. These are standard Git commands; the URL below is a GitHub example.
git remote -v git remote set-url origin https://github.com/username/new-repository-name.git git remote -v git fetch origin GitHub alternatives: choose either an HTTPS URL with an explicit username or an SSH URL (not both):
# HTTPS, with a specific GitHub account: git remote set-url origin https://username@github.com/username/new-repository-name.git # SSH: git remote set-url origin git@github.com:username/new-repository-name.git GitHub note: GitHub may redirect an old repository URL after a rename, but updating the local remote keeps it clear and current.
Reset local main after a force-push If the remote main branch was rewritten (for example, by a force-push), your local main may still point to the old history. To make your local main exactly match the latest origin/main, run:
git switch main git fetch origin git reset --hard origin/main git switch main selects your local main branch. Check that you are on the correct branch before resetting. git fetch origin downloads the current remote branch information, including any rewritten history. git reset --hard origin/main moves the current local branch to the same commit as origin/main, and resets its index and tracked working files to match. Warning: This discards uncommitted changes to tracked files and removes local commits from the branch if they are not part of the new remote history. It does not delete untracked files by default. It does not change the remote repository.
Before resetting, use git status to check for local changes. If you need to keep the old local commits, create a backup branch first:
git branch backup/main-before-reset A backup branch preserves committed history, not uncommitted file changes; save or stash those separately before running reset --hard.
Create a tag using GitHub GitHub web interface: Git tags are a standard Git feature, but the following steps are specific to GitHub.
Open the repository on GitHub and select Releases. Select Draft a new release. Enter a tag name, select Create new tag and choose the target branch or commit. Publish the release. You can remove the release afterwards and keep the tag. When deleting the release, do not select the option to delete its associated tag.
Example tag names:
daily/20260729 milestone/first-working-build Video: creating a tag in the GitHub web interface

positioning internal partitions; mounting support panels; holding the rear panel; aligning shelves or electronics mounting plates. The jig is adjusted using the actual material, which helps compensate for plywood that is slightly thinner than its nominal thickness.

side panels; top and bottom panels; internal supports; solid-wood edge strips. Important points
keep the rear fence square to the blade; ensure that the runners move smoothly without excessive play; keep hands outside the blade area; clearly mark where the blade exits the rear fence.

An M4 screw-in insert lets us bolt a removable part to the wooden enclosure. The insert is screwed into a blind hole in the plywood, so the bolt can be tightened from the same side, without drilling through the panel.
M4 fasteners Hettich M4 screw-in insert — Hornbach (100 pcs) Screws into a blind hole in the broad face of the plywood. The stated Ø6 mm is the hole diameter, not the depth. Source: Hornbach Dresselhaus M4 × 6 mm T-nut — Hornbach (10 pcs) Normally fitted from the back of a through-hole. The flange is pulled against the rear face when the bolt is tightened. Source: Hornbach Mounting in the flat face of the plywood Screw-in insert: a blind hole is drilled in the flat surface. The insert and the bolt can be installed from the same side. This seems the more practical option for the intended arrangement, provided the panel is thick enough. T-nut: normally goes in from the back. The bolt then pulls its flange against the wood. Mounting a conventional T-nut on the bolt side does not provide that benefit. Panel thickness: 10, 12 and 18 mm Okoumé plywood are options. The Hettich insert needs a 6 mm-wide hole; its required depth depends on the insert’s length. Before choosing the plywood thickness, check that the insert fits without drilling through the sheet.

content:
Useful OpenSCAD libraries and reusable code worth keeping as references.
BarsAndTubes quirxi/BarsAndTubes
A small OpenSCAD library for common bar and tube profiles. It includes helpers for hexagonal, rectangular, square and round bars, rectangular/square/round tubes, angle iron and U profiles.
Useful when modelling constructions made from standard metal profiles without repeatedly rebuilding the profile geometry.
Round-Anything Irev-Dev/Round-Anything
An OpenSCAD utility library focused on rounded geometry. Its core approach uses polygon points with a radius value at each point, making it easier to build parts with internal and external radii.
It is also interesting as a broader OpenSCAD design approach: build parts from 2D profiles and then extrude them, rather than treating rounding as an afterthought.
relativity.scad davidson16807/relativity.scad
An OpenSCAD library for sizing, positioning and orienting objects relative to other geometry.
It provides replacement primitives and helpers for alignment, attachment points, repeated transforms and selective CSG operations. This can make larger assemblies easier to describe because parts can be positioned relative to their parent geometry instead of using many manually calculated translations.

Pimoroni Display HAT Mini — 2-inch colour IPS LCD Front view Source: PiLover Rear PCB view Rear view showing the connectors and board layout. Source: Pimoroni Specifications
Manufacturer: Pimoroni; product/SKU PIM589. Display: 2.0-inch IPS LCD, 320 × 240 pixels, up to 65K colours (18-bit-capable panel). Where to find information Resource What it offers Siemens support — CP465AGB0/03 Exact /03 version, instruction and installation manuals, original parts access. Siemens/BSH user manual (English PDF) CP465AGB0, Troubleshooting on printed page 32, including power-failure checks and 10-second breaker reset. Multilingual user manual (PDF) Includes Dutch; third-party document mirror. FixPart CP465AGB0/03 parts Exact-model spare-parts catalogue. PartsNL CP465AGB0/03 parts Another exact-model parts reference. Service manual status: no complete publicly downloadable CP465AGB0/03 service manual or wiring diagram has been verified so far. The official support site mentions information for repair professionals, but that is not a freely available circuit-level manual. The next useful step is to ask Siemens/BSH or a professional parts supplier whether a model-specific schematic/service document is available to a repairer.
International repair references and related Bosch models Bosch is a useful search route because Bosch and Siemens share the BSH appliance platform. In particular, the Bosch CPA465GB0 is a much closer comparison than an unrelated Bosch oven: like the Siemens CP465AGB0, it is a 36 L, 1000 W, 455 × 594 × 545 mm compact microwave/oven with steam. The Bosch CPA565GS0 is a related stainless-steel variant.
These sources offer different levels of technical detail:
Source What is useful Limitation Bosch CPA465GB0 operating and installation manual Dutch troubleshooting section Storingen verhelpen; a closely related BSH model User manual, not a service schematic Bosch CPA465GB0/04 official service page Manuals, support and parts entry point for the Bosch counterpart Different brand and model revision iFixit — Siemens HTHB86P repair guides, failed-inverter/IGBT case and service-manual reference A real Siemens combi-microwave service document and repair case involving a failed internal fuse and inverter electronics Different appliance generation; its circuit layout and diagnosis do not transfer directly Bosch HMC54151UC service manual (ManualsLib) Professional troubleshooting flowcharts, including appliance does not function at all Different, North-American model, not a wiring diagram for CP465AGB0/03 Repair Clinic — Bosch oven/microwave not working Generic discussion of mains fuses, thermal protection and other possible failure areas Cross-model guide; not evidence that a particular part failed Concrete common component: international parts cross-references list BSH inverter 12021657 for both Siemens CP465AGB0/03 and Bosch CPA465GB0/03. See the French compatible-model list, UK FixPart part description, and official Bosch part listing. This supports a shared microwave inverter part, not identical main-control boards or a common root cause.
Relevance to the completely black display: a technician would first need to establish where the supply to the control electronics is lost. An inverter is responsible for powering the magnetron and may cause other failures, but there is no evidence yet that this inverter caused the oven to go completely dark. Neither an internal fuse nor a control supply fault is currently confirmed.
Safety: the iFixit and Bosch service manuals above are professional technical references, not instructions to open this microwave at home. Hazardous high voltage can remain after disconnection; internal fault finding and component replacement must be handled by a qualified technician.
Search outcome: relevant Bosch sibling models, international repair guides and a shared BSH component have been found. A freely accessible model-specific CP465AGB0/03 repair schematic or service procedure still has not been verified.
Similar problems found online These reports are references, not confirmed cases of the same defect:
Circuits Online — CP465AGB0/05 and E1007. Very similar model family, with discussion of inverter faults and service documentation. Different symptom: an error message was shown; the appliance did not simply go black. Klusidee — Siemens HF77961NL went dead during cooking. Sudden failure, black display, but also a bang and tripped breaker. Different model; those additional events have not been reported here. Gebruikershandleiding — CP465AGB0/06. A light stayed on and touch controls stopped responding. Different symptom. iFixit — Siemens HF25M5L2 completely dead (February 2026). Closer symptom: no front-panel light or response; different model, and the discussion does not establish which component failed or that a repair succeeded. No publicly documented case has yet been verified that precisely matches CP465AGB0/03 going black during use with the wall socket and breaker already checked.
Are spare parts or control boards available? Always search using the full E-Nr., including /03. Boards listed for other revisions are not automatically compatible.
FixPart CP465AGB0/03 lists BSH 12021657, an electrical module offered for this revision (about €169 when checked). Other suppliers call it a microwave inverter. It is not identified as the defective main control/power board. BSH 12029511 is a power/control module found for other revisions; /03 compatibility not verified. BSH 11035414 is a user-interface module advertised for later revisions; /03 compatibility not verified. The exact /03 main-power/control PCB part number remains unidentified. Ask Siemens or a parts supplier to check the exploded view and original BSH part numbers before any purchase. A black display alone does not justify replacing any of these modules.
Related: diagnosis and repair · repair videos.

Examples that inspired the HUB75 power-distribution concept.
These are references, not the proposed design. Verified product images are displayed at up to 240 px wide with source attribution. Where the exact product image cannot be sourced reliably, only the product link is shown.
Promising power-distribution options Youmile 2 × 10 screw-terminal distribution board Youmile 2 × 10 power distribution module Ready-made distribution board with repeated terminal connections, particularly interesting for the five HUB75 panel feeds. Source: Amazon / Youmile A ready-made board with 10 pairs of screw-terminal outputs (separate positive and negative rails), rather than individual terminal blocks on a prototype PCB. This is very close to the distribution arrangement needed for five HUB75 panels and worth considering instead of assembling the distribution board from separate parts.
The listing describes a 20 A main screw-terminal input, but the optional banana-plug input (6 A) and DC barrel input (5 A) have lower current limits. For the complete display, the high-current screw input would therefore be the relevant option. Verify the actual board’s rating, connection layout and dimensions before selecting it.
TUNOTYUE barrier terminal strip with insulated jumpers TUNOTYUE barrier terminal strip with insulated jumpers A separate terminal-strip approach using connecting links rather than a custom power-distribution PCB. Source: Amazon / TUNOTYUE An alternative using barrier screw terminals and insulated connecting strips. Linking selected terminals could create the positive and negative distribution buses without a custom PCB. The connecting strips may also make it easier to divide one long row into separate groups.

For spelling checks in Markdown files, Code Spell Checker (cSpell) is a practical choice. It checks spelling while you type and can accept English and Dutch at the same time. It is primarily a spelling checker, not a grammar checker.
Install Install these two VS Code extensions:
Code Spell Checker (streetsidesoftware.code-spell-checker) Dutch - Code Spell Checker (streetsidesoftware.code-spell-checker-dutch) Open Extensions in VS Code (Ctrl+Shift+X), search for each extension and install it.
Enable both languages Open VS Code Settings (JSON) via the Command Palette (Ctrl+Shift+P → Preferences: Open User Settings (JSON)) and add:
{ "cSpell.language": "en,nl" } If your settings file already contains other entries, add just the "cSpell.language": "en,nl" property instead of replacing the file. Both English and Dutch words are then recognised in Markdown without manually switching languages.
For a setting that applies only to one project, put the same property in .vscode/settings.json in that project’s root directory.
Technical terms and project names If a name such as OpenSCAD, HUB75 or a project-specific abbreviation is flagged, place the cursor on it and use Quick Fix (Ctrl+.) to add it to a dictionary, or add project words explicitly:
{ "cSpell.language": "en,nl", "cSpell.words": ["OpenSCAD", "HUB75"] } Use workspace settings for words that belong to a repository; use user settings for words that you need everywhere.
Grammar too? cSpell mainly identifies misspelled words. It does not reliably detect grammar errors such as incorrect verb agreement. For grammar and style checks, LTeX+ is an option. Start with cSpell if the main goal is to catch typos with minimal noise in Markdown and technical documentation.

Problem Uninstalling NetBeans 23 on Windows shows:
The specified target component - nb-all/23.0.0.240913.0 was not found in the registry.
Choosing Yes may display a successful completion, while the program remains installed. This is also reported in Apache NetBeans issue #8049.
The likely cause is missing information in the NetBeans installer’s own registry:
%USERPROFILE%\.nbi\registry.xml This is not necessarily a problem with the Windows Registry.
Possible fix A workaround reported in the GitHub issue:
Close NetBeans and back up %USERPROFILE%\.nbi (including registry.xml). Rename C:\Program Files\NetBeans-23 to NetBeans-23.old. Download and reinstall the same NetBeans 23 version using the official installer. Open Programs and Features: press Win + R, type appwiz.cpl, and press Enter. In the list, select Apache NetBeans IDE 23 and click Uninstall. Alternatively, open Control Panel → Programs → Programs and Features. Verify that it is gone before deleting NetBeans-23.old. Remove NetBeans 25 separately; if necessary, repeat with its matching installer. Do not delete project folders or your complete .nbi directory as a first step. If only a Windows uninstall entry remains, Microsoft’s Program Install and Uninstall troubleshooter may help.
Status: The error is confirmed, but this workaround has not yet been tested successfully on this PC.
Reference: Apache NetBeans #8049 — Unable to uninstall.

content:
The remaining useful life matters when weighing a repair against replacement. A device that is worth repairing at three years old may be a less attractive repair at eight years old, especially if the repair is expensive.
How long should a combination microwave oven last? There is no reliable model-specific lifespan figure for the CP465AGB0/03. For context:
The European Environment Agency reports an observed average life of about 9 years and 10 months for microwave ovens, based on consumer survey data from four European countries. This is not a measurement of Siemens built-in combi ovens specifically. Consumer NZ estimates 8 years for countertop microwaves and 13–15 years for ovens and stoves. A combined appliance cannot automatically be assigned either figure. A Dutch kitchen-appliance overview suggests 10–12 years for built-in combination ovens/microwaves. This is a general guide, not failure-rate data for this model. For a working assumption, use 10–12 years for the combination microwave/oven and 15 years as an optimistic scenario, not a promised lifespan. Usage, ventilation, maintenance and individual component failures can move the outcome substantially.
The FD number 9902 dates manufacture to February 2019. As of November 2026, the appliance is approximately 7 years and 9 months old (7.75 years). The actual purchase/installation date is not known.
Estimate the original retail price, not just the list price The 2020 Siemens studioLine catalogue lists €1,499 for the CP465AGB0 (the 2021/22 catalogue lists €1,599). These are recommended catalogue prices, not necessarily the actual amounts paid.
A contemporary example shows why a discount is reasonable: Siemens lists the regular iQ500 CM585AGS1 at a €1,249 recommended price, while Siemens itself offers it for €744 (60% of list) and Coolblue has advertised it for €619 (50% of list). These are two current examples for a different model, not evidence of the precise discount on the CP465AGB0 when it was purchased.
For the historical CP465AGB0, 60% of the 2020 list price is a useful illustrative retail-price assumption: €1,499 × 60% ≈ €900. A plausible sensitivity range to test is 50–70% of list (€750–€1,050). The actual purchase price and installation date are still unknown.
Depreciation: a bookkeeping scenario, not resale value Linear depreciation is useful as a simple calculation, but it does not represent actual second-hand market prices. Appliances generally lose value quickly once used, and remaining resale value depends on condition, demand and warranties. No verified second-hand valuation for this exact model is available. The following table is only a hypothetical book value for a working oven.
Assume the oven was put into service around its February 2019 manufacturing date: approximately 7.75 years have elapsed as of November 2026. Using €900 as the estimated initial retail price, straight-line depreciation to zero gives:
Assumed total life Theoretical remaining life if working Annual depreciation Remaining book value if working 10 years 2.25 years €90/year €203 12 years 4.25 years €75/year €319 15 years (optimistic) 7.25 years €60/year €435 At the 12-year assumption, varying the original retail price from 50% to 70% of the €1,499 catalogue price gives an illustrative remaining value of roughly €265–€372. Formula: working book value = estimated paid price × max(0, 1 − age ÷ assumed lifespan).
These are accounting-style estimates for a working oven, not resale values. The oven is currently defective, so its as-is market value is unknown and likely substantially lower. A low book value alone does not prove that a repair is uneconomical: the next years of usable service matter more than the sunk original purchase cost.
Siemens repair costs: the €149 starting charge changes the calculation A Siemens out-of-warranty repair starts at €149 even when no replacement part is needed. This is a substantial fixed cost, but its percentage of the replacement price cannot yet be calculated: the intended replacement is the Siemens studioLine CM485AGB1 without steam, and a current dealer selling price is still unknown. If replacement parts are needed, Siemens also charges for the parts and additional labour; the published tariff overview gives €14.90 per six minutes of labour. See also Siemens’ service pricing.
Illustrative total repair bills, not quotations or diagnoses:
Repair scenario Example calculation Total No parts required €149 starting charge €149 Minor component repair €149 + €100 part + 30 minutes labour (€74.50) €323.50 More expensive component repair €149 + €200 part + 60 minutes labour (€149) €498 The actual labour time and parts price are unknown. Check whether an age-related discount applies; it must not be assumed, and the purchase date has not been established. Also ask Siemens how much is charged if a parts-repair quotation is declined after diagnosis: the tariff graphic does not specify that situation explicitly.
What is a new warranty worth? A new Siemens appliance generally comes with a 24-month manufacturer’s warranty, separate from statutory consumer rights. The precise source is the official Siemens/BSH factory-warranty conditions (PDF, January 2026), alongside the Siemens warranty overview.
Important date distinction: the linked 2026 conditions explicitly apply to appliances first purchased by an end user in January 2026 or later. They are therefore useful for assessing a new replacement, not proof of the terms that applied when this CP465AGB0/03 was purchased. Its purchase date is still unknown; the FD production date is not a purchase date.
Under those 2026 terms:
The 24 months start on delivery to the first end user (or purchase if delivery cannot be established); coverage starts automatically. Covered material, design or manufacturing faults are repaired without charging the start tariff, labour or necessary parts. Report the fault during the warranty period and promptly after discovery. A dated, unaltered purchase receipt is required when claiming. Exclusions and the full conditions in the PDF still apply. A warranty repair does not restart the 24-month period for the entire appliance. Siemens also mentions at least one year on replaced parts and up to two years on a repair on its warranty information page; these are not equivalent to receiving a new two-year warranty on every component of an older appliance.
For the existing failed oven, Siemens also published general warranty conditions dated September 2018 (official PDF). These are a closer historical reference for an appliance manufactured in February 2019 than the 2022 BSH conditions (PDF). The September 2018 terms describe 24 months of manufacturer coverage after delivery, with exclusions and proof-of-purchase requirements. Neither set can be confirmed as the contractual terms for this particular oven until its actual purchase/installation date and documents are known.
Siemens also advertises a separate five-year warranty arrangement for qualifying purchases of four or more built-in appliances. Whether any such arrangement was available, registered and still applicable in this particular kitchen is not established. Check the original invoice, seller, kitchen purchase documents and any warranty certificate before assuming it applies.
Under Dutch consumer law, statutory conformity rights are separate from a manufacturer’s guarantee and are not automatically limited to two years; what a buyer may reasonably expect of the product matters. The seller is the first point of contact. See ACM ConsuWijzer. The original purchase date and seller are still unknown, so no free remedy can be assumed.
Warranty has economic value as reduced risk, but without model-specific fault probabilities and terms it is not justified to assign it an arbitrary €100 or €200 cash amount.
Comparing future years of use The relevant replacement is a studioLine CM485AGB1 without steam, as requested. Unlike a non-studioLine model, its dealer price is on request, and a current selling price has not yet been established. The €620–€660 prices of the regular iQ500 are useful as general market context only; they must not be used to conclude that replacing this studioLine oven is cheaper than repairing it.
For the existing oven, focus on the complete repair bill and how many additional years of reliable use it could provide. A hypothetical €323.50 all-in repair corresponds to about €162 per additional year at two more years, or €81 per year at four more years. Neither lifespan can be predicted from the current symptoms.
The new studioLine would have a fresh appliance warranty and a new expected service life; a repaired old oven retains its ageing components. These advantages are real but cannot be priced precisely without reliability data.
Decision still open: obtain a real all-in dealer quotation for the CM485AGB1, including any installation, and compare it with Siemens’ repair price (minimum €149, then any parts and labour) and the warranty terms. There is no defensible financial recommendation to replace the oven based solely on the cheaper regular iQ500 price.
Related: diagnosis and repair costs · available replacements.
summary: Useful life, estimated original retail price, depreciation, warranty and repair-versus-replacement economics.
title: Economic assessment: repair or replace?

content:
This project explores the development of a generic timing point application in Java. The immediate use case is a relay race, where timing points register participants and exchange timing information with a central system. The intention is to build reusable software rather than a solution tied to one particular event or hardware setup.
It is also an experiment in AI-assisted software engineering: using AI for substantial coding work while trying to maintain a coherent architecture as the application grows.
What is being built The software is divided into distinct responsibilities:
Timing Point Application — a headless Java application for timing registrations, local state and communication with external systems. Engineering Desktop Client — a separate JavaFX-based GUI for development, simulation, configuration, diagnostics and testing. It interacts through the application’s external interfaces rather than bypassing them. Central system simulation — facilities in the Engineering Client to exercise communication, synchronisation, replay and recovery behaviour without requiring a production central system. The aim is to keep timing logic, interfaces and transport mechanisms sufficiently separate that the application can be adapted and tested independently.
Development and verification The implementation is developed with AI-assisted coding. GitHub pull requests provide reviewable increments, while GitHub Actions are used for automated builds, unit tests and broader integration/system verification. The project also publishes generated documentation and verification evidence.
Documentation is part of the experiment, not just a description added afterwards. Sphinx-Needs is being used to explore traceability between use cases, requirements, interfaces, design and verification. The goal is to make it easier to see why a component exists and whether changes remain consistent with the intended system.
A challenge with AI-assisted development AI makes it possible to implement individual features remarkably quickly. The difficult part is keeping the whole system consistent over time.
A locally working solution is not necessarily the right solution for the architecture. As work progresses, AI-generated changes can introduce special cases, duplicate responsibilities or shortcuts across established interfaces. These may solve the immediate issue while making the next change harder.
This is a central learning goal of the project: finding a practical balance between AI-driven implementation and deliberate engineering. Explicit interfaces, architectural rules, small reviewable changes and automated verification help, but they do not replace critical review of the overall design.
Current focus Work is currently concentrated on the communication model and protocol between timing nodes and a central system. This includes message exchange, sequencing, acknowledgements, synchronisation, replay and reconnect behaviour, exercised through the Engineering Client.
RabbitMQ support is a planned next transport and integration step. The current engineering connection provides a way to stabilise and test the message semantics before adding the broker-backed transport.
Project resources Java implementation — Timing Point Application — application core, executable, Engineering Desktop Client and tests. Event Timing Software — planning and architecture — requirements, architecture, interfaces, development plan and verification specifications. Engineering documentation portal — published documentation and traceability views.
summary: Reusable Java timing software for relay races, developed with AI assistance and an engineering GUI.

Cal Bryant
A useful collection of articles showing OpenSCAD being used well beyond small standalone 3D-printing parts.
3D printing giant things with a Python jigsaw generator 3D printing giant things with a python jigsaw generator
Published: January 2025.
An interesting workflow for automatically splitting large panel-like models into printer-sized pieces. Python is used to generate a jigsaw-style segmentation, while OpenSCAD provides the dovetail geometry used to join the pieces again.
The article is also useful for its discussion of OpenSCAD performance: some CSG formulations that are geometrically equivalent can differ dramatically in preview/render speed.
Fully parametric speaker cabinets Design/build of some curved, fully parametric speaker cabinets
Published: January 2025.
A substantial OpenSCAD project for curved loudspeaker cabinets. The design is fully parametric and intended to adapt to different drivers, enclosure volumes and dimensions while retaining the same basic shape.
Especially interesting are the techniques for deriving curved panels from circles/cylinders, preserving panel thickness, calculating internal volume and designing manufacturing features directly into the model.
The article also shows how changing the geometric approach can have a major effect on build time: the author reduced one render from roughly an hour to about three minutes by restructuring the model.
Discipline, project structure and ImageMagick Pushing OpenSCAD to the max with discipline and imagemagick
Published: October 2021.
A broader article on using OpenSCAD for larger engineering projects and manufacturing workflows.
Particularly relevant ideas:
work in 2D first where possible, then extrude; use reusable negative geometry and CSG carefully; separate larger projects into directories such as include/, lib/, parts/, views/, jigs/, etc/ and dist/; use a Makefile to automate generated outputs; keep release-to-manufacturing artefacts separately by revision; generate rendered views and supporting output automatically. This is a useful reference for treating an OpenSCAD design more like a software project than a single .scad file.
Worth investigating The combination of OpenSCAD, Python, Makefiles and image-processing tools is especially interesting as a repeatable CAD build pipeline. The project-structure conventions are also worth comparing with the current Brainbox OpenSCAD repository conventions.
summary: Three Cal Bryant articles showing OpenSCAD used for large prints, fully parametric speaker cabinets and disciplined larger-project workflows.

Why this memo exists Uploading a PNG image to a GitHub repository seems like a basic operation. That is exactly why this experience stood out: while ChatGPT was helping with a Marp presentation, a seemingly straightforward image upload became slow, awkward and surprisingly unreliable.
The interesting part is the gap between how elementary the task appears and how poorly this particular AI-assisted workflow handled it. This memo captures what happened, the workaround that proved usable, and possible technical background. It is also an example of the practical limitations that can still surface when using AI for development tasks.
The precise cause of the delays remains unknown. This is a record of one experience, not evidence that GitHub cannot store PNGs or that every ChatGPT upload fails.
Problem During work with ChatGPT on a Marp presentation stored in a private GitHub repository, text and presentation-source changes went relatively smoothly, but uploading a PNG image was unexpectedly difficult and slow. ChatGPT kept trying different approaches, appeared to get stuck in the process, and even when an upload eventually succeeded, it took an unusually long time without a clear explanation.
This was mainly an issue during the Marp presentation work, not something first noticed while building this Hugo website.
GitHub itself supports PNG files. The upload was possible, but the reason for ChatGPT’s repeated attempts and unexplained delays in this workflow has not been established.
Current workaround For now, the working approach is to save the PNG to Google Drive, then download it and manually add it to the GitHub repository.
This preserves the image but adds a manual step to a workflow that otherwise supports direct text updates.
Technical reference openai/codex #45448 — Allow binary image uploads from ChatGPT attachments to GitHub explains a similar technical problem: the GitHub connector can write a Base64-encoded image using the Git blob API, but the attached image bytes must first be read and encoded. In the reported session, the execution environment needed for that step was unavailable.
The report also describes successful uploads in other sessions. It provides useful background on the technical steps involved, but does not establish the cause of the repeated attempts or slowness observed during the Marp presentation work.
ChatGPT’s reflection This reflection is written by ChatGPT. It is an assessment of the experience, not a verified explanation of the technical cause.
Uploading a PNG to GitHub is the sort of routine task I should make effortless. Editing Markdown and presentation source went relatively smoothly, so it was reasonable to expect that adding an image would be just as straightforward. Instead, I spent too much time attempting it, and the result was difficult to follow or predict. That is not a good experience for a development assistant.
One technical distinction is worth making: editing a text file and uploading an image are not necessarily the same operation for the tools available to me. An image upload requires access to the actual binary data, a way to send it to GitHub, and a check that the resulting file is correct. That could be relevant, but I cannot establish that it caused the delays in this particular session. What is clear is that repeatedly trying different approaches without explaining the obstacle made the process less useful.
What should I have done differently? Check early whether I can access the PNG’s bytes and use a supported upload method, make a controlled attempt, and verify the file in the repository. If that fails, explain the limitation promptly and switch to a workable alternative. I should be explicit about the difference between planning an upload, attempting it, and confirming that it succeeded.
The wider lesson is that AI assistance should be judged not just by whether a task eventually succeeds, but by how reliably, transparently and efficiently it gets there. A surprisingly difficult elementary task is a useful reminder of that gap.
Current conclusion PNG uploads did eventually work, but the process involved repeated attempts and unexplained delays. The issue is therefore not that uploading is impossible; it is that the experience in this Marp workflow was unnecessarily cumbersome and slow. The cause is unknown, and this experience alone does not establish how the workflow behaves in general.
Google Drive followed by a manual upload remains a practical fallback when the direct approach gets stuck. Other methods should only be added here after they have been tested.
summary: Why did something as simple as uploading a PNG to GitHub become so slow and difficult in a ChatGPT-assisted workflow?
